# Urrets-Zavalia Syndrome

**Authors:** Majid Moshirfar, Kayvon A. Moin, Yasmyne Ronquillo

**Source:** StatPearls - StatPearls Publishing

## Abstract

In 1963, Alberto Urrets-Zavalia, an Argentinian ophthalmologist, observed 6 patients with fixed mydriatic pupil, iris atrophy, posterior synechiae, and secondary glaucoma after undergoing penetrating keratoplasty for keratoconus. All cases except 1 received topical atropine in this series, and the author suggested that atropine was crucial in causing this clinical condition.  Urrets-Zavalia Syndrome (UZS), also known as Castroviejo syndrome, is a rare and severe complication characterized by a fixed and dilated pupil following various ophthalmic surgeries, sometimes associated with keratoconus or the use of postoperative mydriatic agents. Castroviejo was the first to mention this clinical condition, while Urrets-Zavalia provided a detailed characterization of the condition. Although penetrating keratoplasty is the most common implicated procedure for this syndrome, UZS has been reported following various ophthalmic surgical procedures, including deep anterior lamellar keratoplasty (DALK), Descemet stripping automated endothelial keratoplasty (DSAEK), cataract surgery, and various glaucoma surgeries. Patients usually present with an atonic pupil that does not constrict to light or accommodation. The onset of symptoms varies but commonly occurs 1 to 2 weeks after penetrating keratoplasty. The development of UZS is widely attributed to iris ischemia, which results in subsequent dysfunction of the pupillary sphincter muscles. Although various preventive measures have been attempted, an approved treatment for UZS is not currently available.
